chapters.label: Prologue
chapters.title: An invitation
paragraphs: Every meaningful journey begins with an invitation. Not a plane ticket, not a packed bag, an invitation. Someone saying, come with me.

Most of us spend our days in hallways that are familiar. Then suddenly, a door opens and light spills across the floor, brighter than expected. Shapes start to form. A city street, a child's laughter, a stranger's face. You don't yet know where it leads, but the light itself is invitation enough.
This book is full of those invitations. They're not neat or heroic. They're human, awkward, surprising. None of them are a blueprint. They're simply doors I've walked through.
You won't be asked to copy my path. You'll be invited to notice your own doors, to take a step toward the light.
You don't need all the answers before you begin. You just need enough courage to say yes to the first small invitation.
If you're willing then let's begin the journey together.

chapters.label: Chapter 1
chapters.title: The Red Juice Box
chapters.alt: A small red carton on a stone ledge
paragraphs: The evening settled slowly over Athens. Not all at once. The sunlight softened with every block. But the day didn't let go easily. The heat still rose from the pavement, children ran through small plazas while parents lingered nearby, coffee in hand. Unhurried. The city was winding down, but never fully quiet.
A scooter slipped between two cars with the confidence of routine. Somewhere, dishes clinked behind an open kitchen window.

Between two apartment buildings, the Acropolis appeared again. Only a glimpse. The street curved and it was gone. A block later, it found its way back into view and then, slipped behind the city again. It didn't ask anything of us. It was simply there, a part of the city's skyline.
There were 12 of us walking that night. Some drifting ahead. Some dropping back, never quite in a straight line.
The canvas bag cut gently into my palm. I shifted it to my other hand, the sandwiches rustled inside their clear plastic bags, juice boxes thumped softly against the snack bars.
Earlier that day, those bags had been full, heavy enough to make us laugh at how much we'd packed.

The memory came without warning. A long table, conversations layered on top of each other, hands passing bread down the line, someone sorting juice boxes by flavor. It wasn't heroic or dramatic, just ordinary people preparing a simple meal. No one mentioned changing the world.

And then the memory was gone. We were back on the street. Someone a few steps ahead paused to talk with a man sitting on a low wall. The rest of us slowed without needing to be told. After a few minutes, they caught up. No rush, no concern, just space. Relationships set the rhythm, not an itinerary.

At one intersection, a small neighborhood park came into view. Trees, benches, a patch of green. And then, details that quietly shifted the picture. Discarded syringes near one bench, a folded blanket and a few carefully placed belongings beneath a tree. No one said anything. We just kept walking. Athens rarely separated beauty from brokenness. It simply allowed both to exist on the same street.
I looked around at our group spread out along the sidewalk, and I thought about how little more than a day before many of us had been strangers navigating an airport, 14 hours in the air behind us.
Somewhere along the way, without ceremony, we had started to become companions.

Our bags had grown lighter, sandwiches and juice boxes had been handed out little by little, without much thought, no counting. Just the steady rhythm of the walk. Artur slowed ahead, waiting for us to gather before the next turn. I adjusted the bag and followed.

When I looked up, there was a woman standing directly in front of me. She didn't hesitate. She was already speaking. Fast, urgent words, hands moving as much as her voice. I smiled and said I didn't understand. She didn't understand me either.

She pointed to the canvas bag. I handed her a sandwich, a snack, and a juice box. She accepted the food, then looked at the juice box... shook her head and pushed it back. I tried again, smiling. She pushed it back harder, pointed inside the bag again, her voice rising.
I still didn't get it. I looked into the bag.
Artur came back. He listened, watched, then said quietly, “She wants a red juice box.”
I looked again. Blue, blue, nothing else.
Artur explained. Her voice jumped louder, words sharp even though I couldn't follow them. She pointed down the street, then back at me, then at the bag. Frustration was written all over her face.
Finally, she took only the sandwich, said something loud that I couldn't understand, turned and walked away, voice still sharp in the air.
I stood there with the juice box in my hand. Honestly, I didn't know what else I could have done, and a quiet old thought slipped in.
Sometimes you just get what you get...
It wasn't angry, it just felt reasonable. But underneath that reasonableness was a little knot that I couldn't name yet...
Artur glanced at me for a moment, then nodded. Time to get moving. We did. The city didn't pause just because one conversation had ended, and neither did we.

The bag felt lighter now. Every few blocks another sandwich was gone, another snack bar, another juice box. The streets kept introducing us to people. Some greeted Artur by name. Some just nodded before settling back down onto a piece of cardboard that would be their bed for the night.
One older man beamed when we handed over a sandwich. He held it up like a prize, thanked us with a grin that needed no translation.
A few minutes later, another man accepted the food without even looking up, deep in a conversation we couldn't follow. It wasn't rude, just focused on surviving another night.

One small park was already filling with people laying out blankets, shoes placed neatly by tree trunks, plastic bags of belongings used as pillows. The park was beautiful, and the park was heartbreaking. And somehow, Athens held both of those truths without trying to resolve them.
Somewhere along the way, without consciously deciding to, I stopped thinking about the woman. The walk continued. People came and went. The night kept moving.
By the time Artur quietly let us know it was time to head back toward the apartment, her face, her voice, that moment, had slipped into the background, just one moment among many others.
The city continued. The people were still living on the streets. And the Acropolis still stood at the center of the city.
By the time we got back to the apartment, people settled in. Grabbed some water, found a seat, drifted toward the kitchen. The room felt lived in, easy, not formal.

Stories started to move around the room. Who did you meet? What was it like? Someone talked about an older man who just wanted to sit and talk, someone else mentioned a family in the park. Laughter bubbled from one corner. It was just twenty-five people trying to put an evening into words.
I listened, smiled, replayed little moments in my head.
When there was a natural pause in the room, I heard myself say, "You all are not gonna believe what happened to me tonight." Honestly, I thought I was about to tell the strangest story in the room.

A few heads turned, some smiled. I told them about the woman, how suddenly she appeared, the language barrier, the moment Artur realized what she wanted. And how I couldn't give her what she was asking for. I even caught myself doing the same little shrug I'd given her on the street. A couple of people nodded, someone murmured they probably would have done the same.
Amanda hadn't said much. She was just listening. After a moment she leaned forward just slightly. “Brent…”
“She wanted a red juice box.”
I gave a little laugh. “I know she wanted a red juice box. Of course, I know that.”
Amanda didn't move on. Same gentle voice, same steady eyes.
Amanda looked at me. “Brent.” And stopped.
Just a breath or two, but in that pause something started happening inside me. It wasn't embarrassment or even regret about a bad decision. It was this deeper, quieter realization.
I had always thought compassion was mainly about doing, serving, helping, fixing. And suddenly I saw that before any of that, there's just noticing. Actually seeing a person.
And I hadn't done that. Not out of malice, but out of some quiet habit of turning people into needs, categories, problems to solve.
The weight of it moved through me, not loud, but steady. Like a veil I didn't know was there being lifted.
And Amanda's voice is the one that brought me back. “She just wanted a red juice box.”

chapters.label: Chapter 2
chapters.title: An evening with John
chapters.alt: A weathered wooden bench beside a park path
paragraphs: We followed Artur into the park as the evening light began to thin.

People were already settling around the benches. Beyond the park, Athens kept moving. The streets carried their traffic past the trees, past the people finding a place to sit, past those who would still be there after the rest of the city went home.
We slowed when Artur slowed. Someone stopped to speak with him, and the rest of us found room to wait.

There was something familiar now about the weight of the food we carried. Earlier, we had made sandwiches and gathered small candy bars and fruit drinks for the walk. The preparation was simple enough that our hands could keep working while we talked. Then we picked everything up and went out into the evening, with no way of knowing how long any particular stop might take.

It was June. Almost a year had passed since my first visit to Athens, and I was back with another team. There were streets I recognized, turns that brought back a little of the previous summer. The Acropolis still appeared between buildings as we walked, then disappeared when the road took us another way.
Artur knew far more than the streets. People knew him. He saw many of them almost every night, and as we moved through the park, the walk kept becoming a conversation.
At one bench, he introduced me to a man named John.

John was from England. We began talking, and for a little while the team stood around us. I learned that he had been in Greece for about thirty years. There was more to the story, of course, but we were only just meeting.
Artur looked at me.

“Brent, we have about twenty more minutes of the walk left before we’re done. Would you like to just sit here on the bench with John? We’ll take a little twenty-minute loop and come back by here and pick you up.”
“That would be perfect. I’d love that.”
I sat down.
The group continued through the park. The food went with them, along with the small movements and conversations of people making their way somewhere together. John and I stayed on the bench.

We talked about ordinary things. He told me a little about himself, a little about England. There was no great unfolding of his life that evening. We had twenty minutes, and most of it was simply the sort of conversation two people have when they have just been introduced and find that they enjoy talking.
I enjoyed talking with John.
Before we left that night, I prayed with him. Artur and the others came back, and I joined them for the rest of the evening.
The next night wasn’t my turn to go on the walk.
I asked to go anyway.
I kept thinking about the park. I could remember where the bench was, and I wanted to see whether John would be there. We had barely begun talking the night before. I wanted a little more time.

Once we started out, I spoke to Artur. There were plenty of people to hand out the sandwiches and drinks. Would he mind if I left the group and went straight to the park? When they came through, I could join them again, and we could all go on to dinner.
He thought that was a great idea.
So I went ahead.
This time, I was looking for a particular place. I remembered where we had stopped, where Artur had introduced us, where I had sat while the others finished their walk.
John was there.
He was surprised that I had come back. Pleased, too. He hadn’t expected me to remember him and make my way back to that bench.
I sat down again.
We had longer this time. About an hour, as it turned out, though I wasn’t keeping track of it that way while we talked.

The bench was his office. That was what he called it. People in the area knew he sat there, and they generally left him alone. He had a place, a routine. He usually had a novel he had found somewhere, something to read while he sat through the evening.
Little by little, he told me more.

He had left England years before. He talked about Margaret Thatcher and the direction she had taken the country, how strongly he had disagreed with it. In Greece, he had fallen in love, married, and had a child. Later, the marriage ended.
Thirty years was a long time to fit into a conversation on a bench. I was hearing pieces of it, the parts he chose to tell me as we sat together.

He didn’t trust authorities. That came through in the things he said about work and money, about the arrangements he had made to get through each day. He knew where he would go, what he needed, how late he could stay in one place before moving to another.

He had a spot along the road where people came down from the Acropolis toward the city. People passed him there every day. Some gave him money, and there were regulars he could usually count on. Most days, he made enough for a meal, a small bottle of wine, cigarettes. He managed to keep himself in books, too, and generally had a little money left over.
He told me he would be willing to have a job. But the jobs available to him paid so little that he could make more where he was. He explained it as someone who had already spent time weighing it out.
I listened.

There was a great deal about his life I didn’t know. I had met him the night before. Even now, with more of his story in front of me, whole years lay between the few things I could have repeated back.

Around nine-thirty each night, he left this park for another one. The gates there closed at ten. He slipped in before they were locked and went to a place hidden deep among the trees, where he kept his belongings and slept.
He told me nobody knew where that place was.
His money stayed in the park as well, hidden under a rock. He wouldn’t put it in a bank. He had his own safe place.

As he talked, I began to understand a little of the evening ahead of him. He would sit here for a while longer. Then he would leave for the other park, get through the gates before they closed, make his way to the things he had stored away. Tomorrow, he would go back to his spot near the road.
For now, we still had time on the bench.
He told me about his daughter.
She was twenty-three. He had a granddaughter, too. But his daughter wanted nothing to do with him, and he wasn’t part of their lives.
That hurt him. It came through as he talked about them, about being a father and a grandfather and having no place in their days.
I couldn’t fill in everything that had happened between them. I was listening to John’s part of it, sitting beside him while he told me what it was like to be outside those relationships.
He had let his guard down. The conversation had gone well beyond the few things we had exchanged when Artur first introduced us.
I stayed and listened.
When Artur and the team came through the park, it was time for me to go.

We were heading to dinner. John would stay until it was time for his own walk to the other park. The hour we had spent together had fitted into both of our evenings, and now those evenings were going to take us different places.
I reached out and shook his hand.

I need to admit something here. I have a particular discomfort about shaking hands that are very dirty. I’m not especially fussy about cleanliness in everything else. But that one thing can make me hesitate, and I don’t have a very good explanation for it.
John’s hand was dirty. I noticed. I shook it anyway.
“Hey, John, I’m going to try to come back another night this week. We have a tight schedule, so I don’t know if I’ll make it back. But I’m going to try. I hope I can come back and see you again.”
“Oh, I’d love that.”
I wanted to be able to tell him when. I couldn’t. There were other places we needed to be, other things the team had come to do. I could only tell him I would try.
“So until I see you again, whether it’s in a few days or on a future trip I bring to Athens, take care of yourself.”
He looked at me.
“Brent, the problem isn’t taking care of myself.”
“The problem is loneliness.”
